author: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate

slides.1: Every spring we wait for the rain, and nothing comes. Then the typhoons arrive and drop a whole year of water in two days. Today, let's watch our island cope.
slides.2: SDG 13 is Climate Action. Most people think it only means less carbon gas. It also means cities that survive a disaster, and water that still runs.
slides.3: Taiwan gets plenty of rain. But we are a water-poor island, because our mountains are steep. The rain runs into the sea before we can catch it.
slides.4: Typhoons now come less often, but they hit us much harder. In our worst drought the reservoirs went dry. Rice fields cracked open, and the chip factories nearly stopped.
slides.5: Then the opposite happens. A whole year of rain can arrive in only two days. Our old city drains cannot carry it, so the streets become rivers.
slides.6: So we have to ask a hard question. Can our city water pipes survive another wild season? And can we store the flood water for a dry summer?
slides.7: Taiwan is already working on this. We now have the Forward-looking Water Grid. It joins the pipes of many cities, so Tainan can send spare water to Kaohsiung.
slides.8: Taipei and Taichung are becoming sponge cities. New pavements let the rain soak into the ground. Parks are open and low, so a storm can fill them safely.
slides.9: Our rice farmers are changing too. A computer gives every plant the exact water it needs, drop by drop. This saves millions of tons of water every year.
slides.10: How does STEM help us? Engineers put small sensors inside the water pipes. The data goes to a computer, which finds a hidden leak in minutes.
slides.11: We also make new water. Factories clean their used water until it is pure again. On the coast, new plants take the salt out of sea water.
slides.12: Up in the mountains, we fight landslides too. Instead of tall cement walls, we use rocks and local plants. They hold the soil and keep our rivers clean.
slides.13: But none of this is cheap. New water plants and deep pipes cost billions of dollars. So who pays, and how do we stay fair to ordinary families?
slides.14: There is also a fair-share problem. The rich tech cities get the new water systems first. But small farm villages go dry first, and that is not right.
slides.15: Other islands have the same trouble, and our answers could help them. But Taiwan cannot speak at the big climate meetings. We must share in other ways.
slides.16: One more job belongs to us. We must check that these systems really work, and are not only for show. Every year, ask to see the inspection data.
slides.17: So what have we learned? Taiwan is learning to live with wild weather. Sponge cities, smart pipes and good engineering are making a weak island strong.
slides.18: Why should you care? Because we still need new ideas for better disaster systems. So study science or learn to code, and save every drop at home.
slides.19: Please do not feel helpless here. People are clever, and nature is still very strong. Together they can protect this island, and give our children a safe home.
slides.20: The weather will not wait for us. So will you help us build a safer Taiwan? Together we can be ready, and that work begins today.
